title: Eddie Murphy to Star in Peacock Drama Series ‘The Chairman’ From ‘Mad Men’ Creator Matthew Weiner
description: Eddie Murphy is attached to star in “The Chairman,” a drama series in development at Peacock created by Matthew Weiner. If greenlit, the project wil
body:
Eddie Murphy is attached to star in “The Chairman,” a drama series in development at Peacock created by Matthew Weiner. If greenlit, the project will mark his first-ever role in a live-action scripted series.

	Plot details for “The Chairman” are yet to be announced. The series will be produced by Universal Television and 101 Studios, which is run by “Yellowstone” executive producer David Glasser and is under a first-look film and television deal at NBCUniversal that began in January. “The Chairman” will also be the first project to come out of ex-Paramount boss Chris McCarthy’s deal at NBCUniversal, which was first reported in November 2025 and put him in a consulting role on the studio’s relationship with Glasser and 101. Murphy and Weiner serve as producers on “The Chairman.”
	

	Murphy is among the world’s all-time greatest comedians, having launched his career as a cast member on “Saturday Night Live” for four seasons from 1980 to 1984. Since then, he has focused on comedy specials and movies; his only scripted TV role before “The Chairman” was voice acting on “The PJs,” an animated series he co-created. On the big screen, his credits include the “Beverly Hills Cop” franchise (1984-2024), “Coming to America” (1988), “Harlem Nights” (1989), “Dr. Dolittle” (1998), “Dreamgirls” (2006), “Dolemite Is My Name” (2019) and more.


	Weiner is best known for creating and serving as showrunner on “Mad Men,” which ran for seven seasons on AMC from 2007 to 2015 and is widely regarded as one of the best TV series of all time. He was also a writer and executive producer on “The Sopranos.” Other credits include writing and producing on CBS’ “Becker” (1999-2002) and the 2018 Amazon Prime Video anthology series “The Romanoffs,” which he created.

schema.headline: Eddie Murphy to Star in Peacock Drama Series ‘The Chairman’ From ‘Mad Men’ Creator Matthew Weiner

title: Oscars: International Feature — ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘Fjord’ and ‘Woman Unknown’ Lead Early Contenders
description:
Oct 1, 2026 3:55pm PT	
	

	
	Oscars: International Feature — ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘Fjord’ and ‘Woman Unknown’ Lead Early Contenders
body:
Oct 1, 2026 3:55pm PT	
	

	
	Oscars: International Feature — ‘La Bola Negra,’ ‘Fjord’ and ‘Woman Unknown’ Lead Early Contenders
	



			
			
	
						

									Carla Oset/Netflix
	
					


							
		
	Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change in response to buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.
	


	Best International Feature Predictions Commentary (Updated: Oct. 1, 2026): The submission deadline for the best international feature Oscar has come and gone and now the industry waits to see how many countries are ultimately entering the race.


	While we await the official tally, several contenders have already made their cases on the festival circuit. Spain’s “La Bola Negra” arrives with the TIFF People’s Choice Award, while Cannes has supplied two major players: Palme d’Or winner “Fjord,” representing Romania and the runner-up “Minotaur,” which will compete for France.

	South Korea’s “Possible Love” also has significant momentum after Lee Chang-dong took the directing prize at Venice. And then there’s “Woman Unknown,” Denmark’s selection and the Golden Lion winner, which has perhaps the biggest question mark attached to its Oscar prospects as it still seeks U.S. distribution.

	The list of predictions in all categories can be found here.

	The Governors Awards, which will hand out honorary Oscars to Glenn Close and Ridley Scott, will take place Sunday, Nov. 15. Preliminary voting for the Oscars shortlist in 12 categories runs Dec. 7-11, with the shortlist announcement to follow Tuesday, Dec. 15. Following the close of the eligibility period on Dec. 31, 2026, nominations voting will run Jan. 11-15, 2027. The official Oscar nominations will be announced on Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars will take place on Sunday, March 14, 2027 and will be hosted by Conan O’Brien. The ceremony airs live at 7 p.m. ET on ABC and in more than 200 territories worldwide from the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood.



	

					“Woman Unknown”

title: ‘Fast & Furious’ TV Adaptation Ordered to Series by Peacock, Eyed for 2028 Premiere
description: The “Fast & Furious” TV series, first revealed to be in development earlier this year at the NBCUniversal upfronts, is closer to reality. Peacock an
body:
The “Fast & Furious” TV series, first revealed to be in development earlier this year at the NBCUniversal upfronts, is closer to reality. Peacock announced Thursday that it has greenlit a new scripted television series based on the franchise.

	Vin Diesel, who revealed that a “Fast & Furious” scripted series was in development during the upfront presentation in May, is an executive producer along with One Race’s Sam Vincent (One Race), Original Film’s Neal H. Moritz and Pavun Shetty, and Jeff Kirschenbaum and Chris Morgan.
	

	Mike Daniels (“Sons of Anarchy,” “Shades of Blue,” “The Rockford Files”) and Wolfe Coleman (“Shades of Blue,” “911: Lone Star”) will serve as co-showrunners, pilot writers and executive producers. 


	According to Peacock, the streamer is looking to premiere the “Fast & Furious” series by 2028. 

	Premiere would coincide with the next film installment, “Fast Forever,” which has been slated to hit theaters on March 17, 2028.

	Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group, is the studio. 

	“For the last decade, we have realized that the fans have wanted more,” Diesel said at the upfront in May. “They wanted us to expand the legacy characters, their stories. And for the last decade, the desire has been for us to enter the TV space that Fallon has mastered. And I had to wait till it was right… It became right when Donna Langley started to oversee it all, because that’s when I knew that the integrity of the characters, the international appeal, what makes us all feel like family would be protected in the TV space… The news that I have here today is that Peacock is launching four shows from the ‘Fast and Furious’ universe.”
	

	Previously in TV, Netflix aired the animated series “Fast & Furious Spy Racers” for six seasons between 2019 and 2021.

	In case you’re one of the few out there who doesn’t know what the “Fast & Furious” franchise is about, here’s NBCU’s explainer: “This year marks the 25th anniversary of the launch of one of the most iconic film franchises in cinema history. On June 22, 2001, Universal Pictures released “The Fast and the Furious,” a high-octane thriller set amid the street-racing culture of Los Angeles. The film — starring Vin Diesel as Dominic Toretto, Paul Walker as Brian O’Conner, Jordana Brewster as Mia and Michelle Rodriguez as Letty — would ignite a cultural phenomenon.”

schema.headline: ‘Fast & Furious’ TV Adaptation Ordered to Series by Peacock, Eyed for 2028 Premiere

title: Ynon Kreiz, as Co-CEO of Paramount, to Receive Pay Package Worth More Than $46.5 Million
description: Ynon Kreiz, as David Ellison’s right-hand man at the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery, is getting a big pay bump over his pay package as CEO
body:
Ynon Kreiz, as David Ellison’s right-hand man at the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery, is getting a big pay bump over his pay package as CEO of Mattel.

	Kreiz, 61, signed an initial five-year employment contract with Paramount. He starts Oct. 5, one day before Paramount is set to close its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros.

	Kreiz’s pay package in the first year at Paramount-WB (the official name has not been revealed) will total more than $46.5 million, the company disclosed in an SEC filing Thursday. That includes a one-time signing award of restricted stock units valued at $31.5 million.
	

	By comparison, as CEO of Mattel, Kreiz in 2025 received a total compensation package of $15.1 million (including at $1.6 million salary).

	At Paramount-WBD, Kreiz will receive an annual base salary of $5 million (as of the closing of the merger). He also is eligible for an annual bonus targeted at $4.9 million. In addition to the $31.5 million signing award of RSUs, he will receive 1.25 million shares of the company’s Class B Common Stock (the “pre-closing award”). Also, within 15 days following the WBD closing, Kreiz will be granted RSUs with an aggregate grant-date value of up to $5.1 million (pro-rated based on the portion of the first year of his employment remaining following the merger closing).

	On the first anniversary of his employment, Kreiz will be granted an annual equity award of $20.1 million, according to the filing.

	It’s worth noting that Kreiz’s stock awards (with the exception of the signing award) will vest in equal quarterly installments over a three-year period subject to his continued employment with the company through the applicable vesting date.

schema.headline: Ynon Kreiz, as Co-CEO of Paramount, to Receive Pay Package Worth More Than $46.5 Million

title: Halle Berry Accused of Child Abuse by Ex Olivier Martinez, Who Is Seeking a Restraining Order
description: Halle Berry is being accused of abusing her 12-year-old son by her ex-husband, actor Olivier Martinez, who has filed a petition for a temporary rest
body:
Halle Berry is being accused of abusing her 12-year-old son by her ex-husband, actor Olivier Martinez, who has filed a petition for a temporary restraining order against the actress.

	Martinez alleges that on Sept. 26, the “Catwoman” actress “physically abused our son Maceo, by jumping on him, putting her hands around his neck, and choking him.” Martinez is asking for sole custody, which would amend their current split arrangement. 
	

	The parents have been ordered to participate in confidential mediation to discuss custody, according to an update from TMZ.


	In the request for a restraining order, Martinez contends that there have been “other instances of abuse over the course of the last few years. These other incidents involve additional physical attacks against our son, as well as verbal and emotional abuse from Petitioner to me.”

	For example, Martinez alleges that Berry “told our son that I am ‘a white bitch trying to rob a Black woman’ due to child support issues. Ms. Berry then asked our son, ‘How do you feel about that as a Black man?’”

	Martinez wrote in the filing that Berry had texted him to apologize after the incident. “I do not want topermanently sever the relationship between our son and Petitioner, but I do not believe that they should be interacting with each other until Petitioner can take sufficient accountability for her actions,” he wrote.

	Martinez also asked that Berry be ordered to not be under the influence of alcohol or other substances while conducting visitation with their son. 

	“I believe he may be traumatized by the incident” and does not want to spend time at her house, Martinez said in the filing. 
	

	Berry and Martinez filed for divorce in 2015 after being married for two years. Berry also has an 18-year-old daughter from a previous relationship.

	Representatives for Berry did not respond to request for comment.

schema.headline: Halle Berry Accused of Child Abuse by Ex Olivier Martinez, Who Is Seeking a Restraining Order

title: Venom Frontman Conrad ‘Cronos’ Lant Dies at 63
description: Conrad “Cronos” Lant, the frontman for the legendary Northern British heavy metal band Venom, has died, according to a post on the band’s social med
body:
Conrad “Cronos” Lant, the frontman for the legendary Northern British heavy metal band Venom, has died, according to a post on the band’s social media sites and the Guardian. No cause of death was cited; he was 63.

	“For more than four decades, Conrad’s voice, bass and vision were at the heart of Venom,” reads a statement from the band. “He created something that changed heavy music for ever. Venom never followed the rules. They forged their own path. And Conrad was there at the centre of it all — uncompromising, fearless and unmistakable.”
	

	At the time Venom released its first album in 1981, the group’s imagery — including skulls, bondage gear, swords and all manner of pseudo-witchcraft and Satanism — and flamboyant stage antics were so over the top that many did not take them seriously. But their influence on heavy metal, particularly thrash, was vast and far-reaching, on bands such as Metallica, Slayer, Anthrax and even Nirvana drummer/Foo Fighters frontman Dave Grohl, who collaborated with Lant on the Probot project in 2004. Venom’s album “Black Metal” even spawned the name of a subgenre that has been taken to even greatest extremes by many Scandinavian bands.


	Lant was born in London to a musical family but moved with his family to Newcastle when he was a child. At the age of 16, he joined a band called Guillotine that eventually morphed into Venom; he started as a guitarist, then moved over to bass (which he played for the rest of his career) and finally lead singer as various members left. With their name and image in place, the trio — guitarist Jeff Dunn (who went by Mantas) and drummer Tony Bray (Abaddon) released “Welcome to Hell” in 1981, which featured the single “In League With Satan,” which even included a speech about the devil (recorded backward).
	

	The group continued on that track across five albums during the 1980s, but the one that truly brought them mainstream attention was “Possessed.” Released in April of 1985, the album’s timing coincided perfectly with the rise of the controversial Parents Music Resource Center, led by “Washington wives” Tipper Gore, Susan Baker and others, which testified before Congress about overtly sexual, violent and Satanic lyrics and imagery in popular music. “Possessed” was No. 14 on the organization’s “Filthy 15” songs chart — along with songs by Prince, Madonna, Sheena Easton, Judas Priest and even Cyndi Lauper — and brought Venom’s music to the attention of countless thousands of people who had never heard of them. (The PMRC hearings succeeded in having warning stickers attached to certain CDs and vinyl, but little else except publicity.)

	Venom went on hiatus in 1988 and Lant embarked on a solo career as Cronos throughout the 1990s. But Venom reformed for another seven LPs, the most recent being 2018’s “Storm the Gates.” The band continued to tour right up until this past summer.

schema.headline: Venom Frontman Conrad ‘Cronos’ Lant Dies at 63

title: There Is Precedent for Taylor Swift’s ‘Cleveland!’ Making the World Go Crazy: Paul McCartney’s ‘Silly Love Songs’ Era
description: It is a controversy actually worthy of an exclamation point. When was the last time the internet lost its collective stuff over a single song the wa
body:
It is a controversy actually worthy of an exclamation point. When was the last time the internet lost its collective stuff over a single song the way it did this past week with Taylor Swift‘s “Cleveland!”? And they say there’s no such thing as a monoculture anymore. It might have felt like everyone you knew had not only heard “Cleveland!” (unlike the millions of people coming onto X to proudly proclaim their unfamiliarity with “Choosin’ Texas” as ot busted chart records) but had a Very Hot Take on it. In the realm of her fandom, much of that discourse was defense of the track. But inherent in all that was the idea that the song needed defending. Because at the tip of this social tsunami was a strong supposition that swiftly powered a gazillion Instagram memes:
	

	Love and marriage have made Taylor Swift lose her dang mind… maybe even turned her into the mayor of Simpleton.


	But as the internet increasingly went into pile-on mode about the new song — almost ignoring that she’d simultaneously released three other new tracks, including the new single “Patient Zero,” all of them bringing the old, more morose Swift back to the phone — I began to feel a sense of deja vu. Where had I, and maybe the world, experienced a panic like this before, about an artist whose turn toward silly love longs had been seen as some sort of cultural betrayal, or basic job failure?

	The answer, of course, was in the question. It was Paul McCartney, in the early and mid-’70s, who got besotted with the romantic sillies and asked, “What’s wrong with that?” And further demanded: “I’d like to know!” Because, you know, here he goes… again… giving John Lennon unending nightmares there on Central Park West. It wasn’t just “Silly Love Songs,” which came a few years later on; it was “The Lovely Linda,” the first song on his solo album, announcing that he had traded in the Beatles for matrimony and domestic bliss. His dream had come true, but in the eyes of those who had a different picture of what he ought to be doing, it was more like the dream was over, to quote his ex-partner.
	

	Obviously the author of “Helter Skelter” came through that bout of disapproval over getting ditzy with love pretty unscathed, and so will the author of “Folklore” survive whatever blasts she takes for “Cleveland!” But the accelerant qualities of social media can make the scorn feel much more immediate and wide than the days when the worst McCartney had to face for a while was from Rolling Stone subscribers.

	“Cleveland!,” for anyone not yet keeping score at home, was one of four new songs tagged onto an extended edition of 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl” album, subtitled “The Encore.” The other three were what people have mostly come to expect from the singer, looking back on long-distant relationships with rue and regrets — that she might have treated one of her past loves poorly, in the subtly moving “Pink Clouding,” or that she ever got involved in the first place with guys who turned out to Not Be All That, in “Patient Zero” or “Babylon.”

	The crime of “Cleveland!” wasn’t that she’d created another earworm — which the chorus hook almost undeniably is, if you’ve listened to it more than a couple of times — but that she’d she’d allegedly given up being a poet in the service of no longer being tortured. “Cleveland!” is one of the most prosaic entries in her nearly 300-song catalog, with lyrics that start by recounting recent nasty things that’ve been said against her — that she can’t dance, that she has no ass (that word is blotted out, by the woman who usually has no trouble dropping F-bombs), that she’s gotten old. The other theme is the one where her asslessness doesn’t matter, because Travis loves her anyway. It kind of recalls the songs on “Reputation” where Taylor exulted that her new guy adored her in spite of Kim and Kanye dragging her name through the mud, but this is undoubtedly the bubblegum version of that, between the hyper-cheery arrangement and no real recent scandal to react to; it pivots on the admittedly questional idea that her new husband is noble for cherishing her even though she’s only a better dancer than 99.9999% of the planet.

	Throw in a spoken-word section — which gave some people PTSD, bringing up the repressed memory of the spoken bit from “Me!” that she actually eventually excised from that recording — and it was a recipe for much of the public to start piling on. Now, I was on record within a couple hours of the tune coming out last Thursday night as not minding the song, saying anyone who’s truly and madly in love deserves an outlier goofball moment in the course of their honeymoon phase. But some of the reactions were funny, the ones that were just amused instead of morally stricken. I LOL-ed at one meme I saw on Instagram, captioned “What happens when Taylor writes about Travis,” which pictured a young woman repeating phrases like “He’s my man… my man… MY man” while looking up Cleveland Heights on Wikipedia.
	

	Swift had set her fandom up for this dichotomy when she filmed a conversation with Harvey Mason Jr. at the Grammy Museum a few weeks ago, before the amended album release was announced. She said then, “I think that the way that I’ve chosen to express myself as a lyricist has changed over the years, and there are times when like those contradictions will come up where fans will be like, ‘I can’t believe the same person who wrote this wrote this.’ Because one will be very simplistic and silly, and one will be very detailed and deep and we’re doing tons of allegory, and we’re just in a whole other world of atmospheric speech. But I think that that human contradiction is fun. I think that it’s fun to make playful songs. I think it’s fun to make songs that are desolate and lonely and just bedraggled lyrically as well.” Swifties assumed she meant to explain the difference between “Ruin the Friendship” and “Wood,” when really she was warning everyone that a song as exquisite as “Pink Clouding” would soon be juxtaposed with the unrepentant bluntness of “Cleveland!”

	This all came to fore, for me, the other night when I went to an L.A. FYC screening of the Paul McCartney & Wings documentary “Man on the Run.” The middle of the movie goes deep into some of the resistance that critics and fans — an estranged Lennon at the top of the list — put up when songs about Linda became the focus of his attention, with an initial folky musical single-mindedness to match. Granted, McCartney already had a reputation as the Beatle who counterbalanced Lennon’s darkness with the extreme fizziness of a “Honey Pie” or “Your Mother Should Knows,” but he also had a quality of depth on his permanent record as the author of “Yesterday,” “Eleanor Rigby” or even, then very recently, “You Never Give Me Your Money.” Now he, Linda and the sheep were on seemingly the world’s most extended honeymoon, with moony music to reflect it. And for some dismayed fans, it only got worse from there, from McCartney tap-dancing on a TV special to putting out “My Love” as the embodiment of what would come to be known as adult contemporary.

	Lennon dragged his ex-collaborator in interviews that bordered on the vicious, leading Paul to respond in song with “Too Many People,” before Lennon dug in further and better with the ultimate diss track, “How Do You Sleep,” taking the position that McCartney should rightfully be kept awake at night by the haunting thought of having become such a lightweight.
	

	Lennon’s rejoinders hurt McCartney’s feelings so terribly badly that he went on to write and record “Silly Love Songs,” a sweet-faced F-you to Lennon and anyone else who’d objected to the previous few years of objectifying Linda as his true lady madonna.

	So… Taylor Swift in 2026 as Paul McCartney in 1971? The analogy gets more complicated when we consider that, at times, Swift has been more of a John than a Paul, actually. (Then again, there were moments when Paul was more of a John, too, but that’s a digression for another day.) Swift’s brutal, bitter takedowns of not just some of her former loves but former business partners or industry enemies in some of the darker passages of “Folklore” could legitimately be characterized as Lennon-esque. And that was not so many years after the decidedly Paul-like “Shake It Off”… and not so many years before she began writing about her future husband with “So High School,” the pep-rally outlier on the otherwise fantastically depressing “Tortured Poets Department.”

	As a lifelong McCartney fan, when rifling through his catalog, I’ve often skipped over “The Lovely Linda,” “My Love” (unless it got to the brilliant guitar solo, and then I was inexorably hooked) and “Silly Love Songs.” Yet I never shunned them entirely, and I was happy they existed. Similarly, in the week that the extended “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore” has been out, I’ve played three of the four new tracks a good deal, while I have saved “Cleveland!” for, uh, special occasions. It’s never going to be a favorite, but it’s never going to feel like a moral affront, either. It’s always been my position that people ought to get at least a partial pass for the things they say and do in the immediate throes of a new love, or in the first aftermath of a breakup — it’s those extreme reactions that make the world go round. You can love that she’s in love without having to love the latest song that came out of that altered state… or without having to demonize it, either. (Especially when it’s, you know, a bonus track?)

	In the bigger picture, perhaps we could listen to what the man said: Love doesn’t come in a minute. Sometimes, it doesn’t come at all. Those lines have always struck me as deep and resonant, weirdly, in a song that’s otherwise anything but.
	

	In the meantime, back in inflammatory meme-land… To quote the sage poet who wrote the previously most famous song about Cleveland, Randy Newman: Burn on, big river, burn on!

schema.headline: There Is Precedent for Taylor Swift’s ‘Cleveland!’ Making the World Go Crazy: Paul McCartney’s ‘Silly Love Songs’ Era

title: ‘Bachelor’ Producers Send Legal Threat to Chris Harrison’s New Dating Show ‘The Vow’; Fox Nation Fights Back ‘Malicious and Vindictive’ Claims
description:
Warner Bros. TV and Fox Nation are butting heads over the latter’s upcoming series, “The Vow,” hosted by former “Bachelor” host Chris Harrison.

	In
body:
Warner Bros. TV and Fox Nation are butting heads over the latter’s upcoming series, “The Vow,” hosted by former “Bachelor” host Chris Harrison.

	In the letter obtained by Variety, sent Sept. 18, WBTV, the studio that produces “The Bachelor,” sent a cease and desist to Fox Nation, claiming the new series appears to be, through promos, “a plain attempt to capitalize on and ‘ride on the coattails’ of WB’s instantly recognizable intellectual property and the Franchise’s goodwill in violation of, inter alia, state and federal trademark, copyright, and unfair competition laws. Without having seen the Series itself, we cannot comment on it and reserve all rights in connection therewith. To be clear, though, we have no objection to Fox and Lionsgate releasing a dating show hosted by Chris Harrison in and of itself. But thus far, Fox and Lionsgate have promoted the Series entirely on the back of the Franchise, not on its own merits.”
	

	The legal note, with the subject line, “Cease and Desist regarding The Vow – Unauthorized Use of THE BACHELOR Intellectual Property,” says that the marketing around the new series “capitalizes on WB’s intellectual property and goodwill in the Franchise,” before listing “Non-exhaustive examples of your unauthorized use” in the form of screenshots of the trailer and screenshots from past seasons of the franchise.


	For example, WBTV calls out the red roses appearing in the trailer, saying, “Red roses are, of course, one of the central and instantly recognizable symbols of the Franchise, and this image from the Series teaser is plainly a direct copy of numerous Franchise promotional materials.”
	

	They also claim that the thumbnail appears to “feature a mansion in the background meant to evoke the iconic ‘Bachelor Mansion.’ “

	Fox Nation responded in a letter on Sept. 24, writing that WBTV does not hold any rights over “falling roses motif or in the words “The Bachelor” when used colloquially to describe a single man.” The note, obtained by Variety, continues, “Your letter also focuses myopically on certain stills from the trailer, while omitting that its clear purpose is to convey that The Vow ‘offers a different approach’ from other dating shows ‘by placing the focus on meaningful relationships, commitment and building a life together.’ Your letter appears designed not to vindicate legitimate copyright and trademark interests, but to restrict FOX Nation and Chris Harrison from promoting a competing dating show. It is unfortunate that Warner Bros. is targeting Mr. Harrison in this malicious and vindictive manner.”

	Fox Nation also notes that “falling rose petals are scènes à faire — stock elements long associated with the romance genre that have featured in films from ‘American Beauty’ to ‘Moulin Rouge’ to ‘Beauty and the Beast.’ Warner Bros. cannot keep for itself a trope it has borrowed from others.”

	Their response ends with a callback to the new series’ catchphrase: “‘The Vow’ exhorts its participants and viewers to ‘Choose Love.’ We trust Warner Bros. will do the same and drop its pursuit of these meritless claims.”

	“The Vow” is set to premiere on Nov. 11, with six episodes rolling out weekly, following eligible bachelor  Jace Cates’ journey dating 10 women. Per the official description, the show will explore “whether shared values, faith, communication, and long-term goals can build a relationship designed to last long after the cameras stop rolling. At a time when much of modern dating culture is driven by fleeting connections and social media attention, the series offers a different approach by placing the focus on meaningful relationships, commitment and building a life together.”

	Harrison hosted “The Bachelor” and its many spinoffs from the series’ inception in 2002. He had a controversial exit from the franchise in 2021.

title: ‘Landman’ Season 3: Colm Feore, Mustafa Speaks, Bobbi Salvor Menuez, Francesca Xuereb Promoted to Series Regular Status
description: “Landman” Season 3 is officially in production, with the hit Paramount+ oil industry drama promoting four cast members to series regular status.
body:
“Landman” Season 3 is officially in production, with the hit Paramount+ oil industry drama promoting four cast members to series regular status. 

	Colm Feore (Nate), Mustafa Speaks (Boss), Bobbi Salvor Menuez (Paigyn), and Francesca Xuereb (Cheyenne) have all been promoted going into the new season, which is shooting in Fort Worth, TX. 

	Billy Bob Thornton leads the cast of the series, which also includes Demi Moore, Andy Garcia, Ali Larter, Sam Elliott, Jacob Lofland, Michelle Randolph, Paulina Chávez, Kayla Wallace, Mark Collie, and James Jordan. As previously reported, Michael Kelly is joining the show’s third season as a series regular. 
	

	Taylor Sheridan co-created “Landman” with Christian Wallace. Both are executive producers along with David C. Glasser, David Hutkin, Ron Burkle, Bob Yari, Christian Wallace, Thornton, Geyer Kosinski, Michael Friedman and Stephen Kay. Dan Friedkin and Jason Hoch for Imperative Entertainment, and J.K. Nickell and Megan Creydt for Texas Monthly also executive produce. “Landman” is produced by Paramount Television Studios, 101 Studios, and Sheridan’s Bosque Ranch Productions.


	“Landman” has proven to be a major hit for Paramount+. According to Nielsen multiplatform data, the series averaged over 14 million viewers an episode in the first five weeks of 2026.

	Spoilers ahead. 

	At the conclusion of the second season, Tommy (Thornton) has been fired by Cami (Moore) as the head of M-Tex. Rather than take on a new job at another oil company, Tommy decides to bet on himself by going into business with his son (Lofland), which forces him into business with cartel boss Gallino (Garcia).

schema.headline: ‘Landman’ Season 3: Colm Feore, Mustafa Speaks, Bobbi Salvor Menuez, Francesca Xuereb Promoted to Series Regular Status

title: Chris Hansen Confronts ‘Primetime’: The Tragic Ending, Seeing His Love Life Onscreen and Considering Legal Action Against A24 Because ‘They Exploited Me’

body:
“Primetime” is a box office overachiever, but the subject of the A24 film calls it a “complete work of fiction.”

	Lance Oppenheim’s movie centers on “To Catch a Predator,” the popular “Dateline” segment that ran from 2004 to 2007. In the show, an advocacy group with adult decoys posing as children would chat with online predators in order to lure them to a house, ostensibly to have sex with a minor. But instead of their prey, they would be met by host Chris Hansen (played by Robert Pattinson), who would interrogate the predators about why they were pursuing illicit and illegal affairs. The suspects were then arrested by law enforcement waiting outside the house.
	

	The film is based more specifically on the 2009 Esquire article “Tonight on ‘Dateline’ This Man Will Die,” which chronicled an episode of the show involving Louis William Conradt Jr., an assistant district attorney in Murphy, Texas, who died by suicide after being caught in a police sting conducted in coordination with the “Predator” team.


	Hansen is continuing his work on his media platform, TruBlu, which hosts shows such as the spiritual successor to “Predator,” “Takedown With Chris Hansen,” which launched in 2022.

	Variety spoke with Hansen a few days after he watched “Primetime.” He discussed his perspective on its box office success, which parts are most upsetting to his former colleagues and what legal action he might take against A24.
	
		Did you have the sort of mentorship with any of the decoys, as it’s portrayed in the movie?	

	No. The only elements of the movie that are not fictionalized are the fact that he uses my name and two or three catchphrases. Everything else is fictionalized. Yes, there was an assistant DA who tragically took his own life, but the circumstances surrounding it, the timeline, the events, it may be based on reality, but none of it is truthful. It’s a complete work of fiction.
	
	
		The whole movie leads up to the 2006 suicide of Louis William Conradt Jr., and the movie version of Chris Hansen has a big meltdown after it takes place. What was going on in your head as that happened? Looking back on it now, are you processing it differently?	

	Look, nobody wants to see somebody take their own life. But in this case, you had a public official, an assistant district attorney who prosecuted criminal cases, who, according to the police and evidence gathered in the case, conducted sexually explicit conversations with decoys posing as two different teenage boys. In Texas, like many other states, that constitutes a felony. Now, he didn’t show up at the house, but the police made a decision to get a warrant based on probable cause. And I think if you were to talk to the police making those decisions, they would tell you that there was some concern that evidence might be destroyed and that they were going to go serve that arrest warrant at his home.

	Now, obviously, we knew they were gonna do this, and we captured the action from the street. And when they went in, according to Murphy police, he had a gun in his hand. He said, “I’m not going to hurt you guys,” and took his own life. Later, Texas Rangers did an investigation, and they determined that on that computer from which he was trying to extract the hard drive, there was child sexually abusive material. As a prosecutor, he knew that in Texas, you could potentially face 10 years in prison for each of those images. So nobody can tell you exactly why Bill Conradt took his own life. Nobody wanted to see it happen. It’s tragic for his family. It’s tragic for him. But to insinuate that there was some push on our part to go arrest him or get him or to find him or to cajole him, it just didn’t happen. He surfaced like any other alleged predator did in an investigation. The decoys don’t go try to find them. They conduct the investigation, and they find us.

	The rules on it are very, very explicit. But we have caught a number of high-profile people. We were in San Francisco on a sting last month, and an Ivy League-educated lawyer who ran a multimillion-dollar investment fund showed up in the middle of the day to sexually exploit a 6- and 13-year-old boy whose father he thought was going to take part in the sex act. We don’t look for people; they find us. The whole premise of the movie is false. It’s a fake narrative. It didn’t happen. If that was the case and the police wanted to make a big splash publicitywise, wouldn’t you think they’d wait till Monday when he was sitting in his office at the district attorney’s office and barge in and get him and walk him out of there? That’s what they would have done. Everybody wants to say that this was done for clicks and ratings, and it wasn’t; it was just part of an investigation.
	

	If anybody would take a moment, as some content creators have, and actually look at the story that we did on that particular case, and look at what we did on “The Today Show” the next morning, we were painstakingly transparent about what happened, how it happened and, as much as we knew, why it happened, as we have been with this franchise from the very beginning, continuing through today when we do these investigations which we now call “Takedown With Chris Hansen.” Any sense that anybody involved was pushing forward or that there was a ratings-hungry producer, none of that is true. Even the notion of the name of the film, “Primetime” — “Dateline” has always been on primetime television. It wasn’t like it was at 2 o’clock in the morning, and we were trying to get it on primetime. It was always on primetime. No discussion in that film ever happened.
	
		“Predator” launched on “Dateline,” which is a journalistic platform, but do you look at your work as journalism or advocacy or something else?	

	There are people who think that we have historically worked too closely with law enforcement. But my argument is that’s the only way to be socially responsible and to ensure that there’s justice served in these cases. In the first two investigations, we didn’t collaborate with law enforcement. We didn’t know what was going to happen, but it became very clear in the third investigation that we needed to have a law enforcement presence. That has evolved over the past 22 years into what I think is the best possible way of doing this. That is to ensure justice and to ensure the chain of custody of evidence is secure. And also, look, it doesn’t matter how horrifying the crime is, everybody in this country is entitled to a vigorous defense. So the materials that we capture, obviously, everybody has access to that. Whether you’re the prosecutor or the defense, everybody deserves their fair day in court.
	
		“Primetime” focuses on the show, but it dips into an understanding of your personal life and love life as seen through tabloid media. How did you feel seeing it in the film?	

	It’s par for the course. You know, even the filmmakers will tell you that this is fiction. And, you know, even when something reflects potentially a real-life event, the timeline has shifted around to make it work in the narrative of the filmmaker. But again, the timeline and the narrative and all of it is fiction. And so, the motives and everything that is detailed in the film, none of that actually happened the way it’s depicted. For them to do that, what’s the motive of making that film? A lot is being made of that right now. What does that say about Hollywood? If you’re gonna make a fictional film, why do you use my name?
	

	The reason you use it is because I’ve spent 45 years creating a very valuable brand, and they wanted to exploit it. They know that if they use the name “Chris Hansen,” people will come to the movie. Most of them will understand the movie is fiction, and there’s a graphic at the end of the film saying so. But that’s not the way it’s portrayed in the beginning of the film. And because there was such an attempt to imitate — although I think it was way more dramatic and over the top — my mannerisms and my lines and things I’ve said over the years, they turned it into a science fiction film, almost, with the greens and the vampire look of the character. It’s just over the top. In fact, it was so over the top, I was left wondering, “What’s the point of this?” And again, I’m not objective, because they exploited me and my brand and my name image for commercial enterprise. But a lot of people don’t think that’s fair. A lot of people think that’s identity theft in one way or another.
	
		What do you think the filmmakers’ larger point about media and Hollywood was?	

	I don’t know. I mean, I’ve invited the filmmaker, Lance Oppenheim, on my podcast to talk about the film. I’ve invited both him and Robert Pattinson to come on. And look, Robert Pattinson’s a very good actor. And I think a lot of people would find it flattering that this guy would be cast to portray me. But the way it was done is certainly not flattering. And so what’s the larger point for Hollywood here? I mean, there are people who would point out that this is an industry that was run by one of the most prolific predators who walked the planet, Harvey Weinstein. And so you can’t take that out of the equation. Maybe that was an influence, not Harvey Weinstein himself, but maybe that attitude in Hollywood was an influence here? Maybe not. I don’t know what the motive is. You ask Lance Oppenheim, and he’ll tell you that this is an interpretation of the internet’s interpretation of another interpretation of Chris Hansen. What does that even mean? I’m a pretty bright guy. I’ve been an enterprise reporter for 45 years, around the world in dangerous places, and had to unravel some very, very difficult mysteries. But I don’t know what he’s talking about. And I don’t think I’m the only one.
	

	I think Hollywood gets in these circles of buying into what they think is some sort of brilliant creative take on something that’s very good and positive and has created a lot of awareness and dialogue in this world. And they’ve twisted it into something that it’s not. And when [Oppenheim] is asked about the ethics of using my name, image and likeness without any input or consult or consideration, he says, “They made ‘The Odyssey’ without talking to Homer.” And that’s what they’re going to go with. I mean, that’s kind of a stretch there. So that’s their belief. I think they get into this Hollywood mindset where “Guys, guys, I got an idea. Let’s do this.” “Oh my God, that’s genius.” And one thing leads to another. I’m not advocating that people don’t go see the movie. I’m just saying that they need to know that it’s completely fiction.
	
		With the buzz around the movie, what’s the reaction you’ve heard from the general public?	

	I think people understand that the movie is fiction. When I went to go see the movie in New York at the theater at Times Square, we interviewed moviegoers who were quite shocked that I was sitting in the back row of the theater with them as they’re watching the movie, unbeknownst to them. It was an interesting moment. But the initial response is what the response has been all along, which is obviously this is fiction.

	People often ask me, “What have you left on the editing room floor? What have we not seen?” My answer is “You’ve seen everything.” We’ve been painstakingly transparent about our methodology, from the very beginning, and continue to be today. So you see everything that happens, and nothing is held back. So you can make your judgment whether you like it or not, or however you feel about it, but we are honest about our methodology. Always have been, always will be.
	
		The movie had a strong opening at the box office. How do you process that?	

	Look, I think A24 is a hot studio right now, and they had one of the most bankable actors in Hollywood today. So those two things are going to drive people initially, at least, to see the film. It doesn’t surprise me that it does well. Look, we bought ads for TruBlu that run in the theaters before that movie is shown in virtually every theater in America. We spent a substantial amount of money to do it, but I think it’s paid off.
	
	
		Are your friends and family seeing the movie?	

	Well, my wife went with me, and we watched it together. And the takeaway was it’s so bizarre and over-the-top fiction that it was hard to get upset about it, because it’s ridiculous in so many ways. My kids, I don’t think they’ve seen it yet. Maybe they’ll wait till it comes out on cable. The extended family, I don’t think they have feelings either way. They’ll maybe catch it, maybe not. They don’t like the way it was done, and I don’t think there’s a tendency to support somebody who would do that.
	
		You’ve spoken about the Jeff Zucker cameo. Have you texted him to ask, “What was up with that?”	

	No, I need to check in with him. You know, Jeff was my first executive producer at NBC when I started there. And look, those conversations never took place. Jeff never said that. And I had nothing but a warm, constructive relationship with him his entire time at NBC. I’ve run into him socially a little bit over the years, and when he was at CNN, I was over there doing some stuff, but none of that ever happened. It was just silliness.
	
		What was your departure from NBC like?	

	It was time to move on. I spent 21 years at “Dateline,” and I had an incredibly good run there. I think the show was changing into more of a murder mystery procedural. And they do a phenomenal job there. And [correspondents] Keith [Morrison] and Josh [Mankiewicz] and Dennis [Murphy] are all good friends of mine to this day. But I had opportunities to go do different things and explore other possibilities. That journey led me to essentially have my own network and my own platforms with three generations of followers, viewers and listeners. For a guy who’s been doing this as long as I have, it’s the absolute best-case scenario to have the exposure and the platforms I have. It’s very rewarding and gratifying that my work is still seen and respected and that we have the energy and passion to go out and do it, and I’ve got a phenomenal team at TruBlu with whom I do it.
	
		Are there co-workers from the “Predator” days that have reached out in the wake of all this?	

	Oh yeah, they’re all upset.
	
		What’s upsetting them the most?	

	It’s upsetting them that they’re unfairly portrayed, especially the producer, who NBC will not allow to talk about this. The press department won’t. But I mean, she’s understandably upset because of the way she’s portrayed and the way I was portrayed. I’ve never yelled at a colleague ever. I think that goes to why A24 never reached out. They had a vision of what they wanted this character to be, and they were afraid if they talked to me or talked to anybody who knew me well, they’d find out I’m a really nice guy who’s a good dad and goes out and works very hard every day to create content that’s important to people. That’s not what they wanted.
	

	So that’s why, in spite of an outreach earlier by a colleague of mine who knew how to get in touch with Lance Oppenheim — he reached out, and Lance texted back that “It’s a love letter to Chris Hansen, and we’ll be in touch soon.” This was nine, 10 months ago. I thought after seeing the film, “If that’s a love letter, I’d hate to get a poison pen letter from this guy!” It ranges from just being wholly offended that anybody would portray us in that manner to my security guy, Ronnie Knight, saying, “I’ve never seen you drink from a straw” — from the silly stuff to the important stuff.
	
		You’ve mentioned the potential of taking legal action against “Primetime.” Is that still being considered?	

	You know, look, it’s a full-time job being the real Chris Hansen. I haven’t really delved in. There are lawyers looking at it, and I think some of them are itchy to make a statement and challenge some things here, but there’s no rush to do that. I’ll have some meetings in the near term, and we’ll discuss it. But I’m really in a great place with everything I’m doing and in my life, and I don’t know how it could be any better. I’m blessed. So do you make that stand? I certainly wouldn’t have done it prior to the film, because I think part of their reasoning behind the way they’ve handled this was to try to get me to be upset and try to do something, and then it becomes “The movie Chris Hansen doesn’t want you to see!” There are those who think that was part of the promotional plan here. Again, it’s something I have not ruled out, but we’ll take a close look at it in the near future.
	
		Has there been an influx of visitors to TruBlu in the wake of the film’s buzz?	

	In terms of people seeing the new work on TruBlu, yes, that’s happened. You know, they see the documentaries we produced on Roblox and sextortion, and there’s another documentary that was produced called “I’m Chris Hansen” which was in the works before the film. I cooperated in it, but I didn’t have editorial control over it. We knew about the film. And that should be out soon. But that’s more of a personal biopic documentary.
	
		Have any former predators ever reached out to you and the team and said, “I feel like I’m rehabilitated, and I wanted to thank you for showing me rock bottom?”	

	Yeah, that has happened. In fact, it happened in Michigan with a doctor who was caught in a sting. He had engaged in a daylong chat with a decoy posing as a 15-year-old girl as he was seeing 18 patients. He sent explicit pictures, showed up at the sting house with wine and cookies and the whole thing, patted her on the behind as he walked in. And we confronted him. It was a very dramatic, long interview, and he had a health issue in the middle of it. And so EMS were brought in. After, he went through the criminal justice system. He got probation and registration as a sex offender. He sat down with me and did an hourlong interview. There’s the most recent example.
	

	But yes, people have reached out, and some of them have not wanted to go public. I do two podcasts — one is “Predators Uncaught,” where we go back over these cases. And the other one is “Have a Seat With Chris Hansen,” where we do a lot of different topics. You can see that interview with the doctor, and he comes clean with his wife sitting in the room as he’s doing the interview. It’s quite something. Now, this is a guy who had no child porn on his phone. He had no previous history, but he talks in great detail about his porn addiction and how that led him down this road to the point of being arrested in a standing with the Genesee County Sheriff’s Office.
	
		As someone who’s spoken to so many of these individuals, do you think there is a path to redemption for some of them?	

	I think for some people, if there’s an intervention when they’re young, if there’s a commitment to not reoffend, to dig deep in therapy, there is redemption. I hear stories about these people, and I have men reach out to me and say, “Look, you need to know that I was in this situation. I don’t necessarily want to go on your podcast and talk about it and be identified, but you need to know that this can happen.”

	I believe for some people it can, but for the larger majority … Look, these guys are not all the same guy. We want one-stop, easy solutions in our society to say, “OK, lock them all up. In some states, castrate them in severe cases, life in prison, death penalty in Florida, severe child sexual assault case.” And all of that is warranted in different cases, but they’re not all the same guy. So the challenge for the criminal justice system is to determine who can be rehabilitated. And that’s why they have the sex offender registry, because at least when these guys finish with their punishment, you can track them and where they are, and they have to report, and they have to be held accountable. So it’s a system that usually works. It’s not perfect. But the unsung heroes on some of this are the parole and probation officers who’ve got to keep track of these guys. It’s a challenging job and it’s certainly not a glamorous job, but it’s an important job.

	NBC did not respond to Variety‘s inquiry about Hansen’s assertion that its press department barred a producer from speaking out about the film. However, a spokesperson for the network shared a statement about the film: “The movie is a fictionalized portrayal of events from nearly two decades ago that were extensively reported at the time. Over its nearly 35-year history, ‘Dateline’ has significantly evolved along with the television landscape.”
	

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: Chris Hansen Confronts ‘Primetime’: The Tragic Ending, Seeing His Love Life Onscreen and Considering Legal Action Against A24 Because ‘They Exploited Me’

Christa Pike
                          Laid Out Alleged Childhood Abuse ...
                          In Bid To Get Off Death Row
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 1, 2026
                            4:15 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Christa Pike claimed she was the victim of horrific childhood abuse at the hands of relatives as she fought to get taken off death row ... and her allegations are horrifying.
      
    
            TMZ obtained court docs from previous appeals in her murder case in which the convicted murderer laid out the abuse she claims to have suffered in her childhood ... and it's a lot to take in.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Christa, who was fighting to be taken off death row at the time based on ineffective assistance of counsel, claimed the court had not considered the abuse and neglect she suffered ... including sexual abuse from multiple abusers and her placement in juvenile facilities where she said the "semblance of continuity and stability actually caused her to sabotage her own chances of going home."
      

            Her legal team said prosecutors painted her as an "out-of-control" teen in proving their case that she murdered Colleen Slemmer in 1995 in a jealous rage over a boy. They brought up another alleged incident where she attacked her mom's boyfriend with a butcher knife. Christa said prosecutors failed to mention that the boyfriend in question had been wrestling and pinching her nipples.
      
    
            In addition, Christa's team claimed she was physically abused by her father. Her dad denied the claims, but she claimed photos that emerged after trial showed she had visible scars from his alleged abuse.
      
    
            Christa said she was raped by four different men and sexually abused by another. She claimed she was sexually abused as a toddler… and once was thrust into a chicken coop, had the door locked behind her, and left to fend for herself in the dark while spiders crawled over her skin.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In addition, she claims she was violently assaulted and raped a year before she murdered Colleen.
      
    
            Her bid to get off death row has so far come up short. As TMZ previously reported, Christa was injected with two lethal doses on Wednesday, but she did not die. She is currently hospitalized in Tennessee.

                                                                      |

                                  October 1, 2026
                                12:55 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Chris Brown's former housekeeper has agreed to accept a lower damages award in her dog bite case against the singer after a judge gave her a choice -- accept the reduced amount or take the risk of a new trial on damages.
      
    
            In court docs obtained by TMZ ... Maria Avila -- who claimed she was viciously attacked by Brown's dog in his Tarzana home in 2020 -- agreed to the new $9.5 million in damages.
      
    
            Avila initially won a $12.9 million judgment ... but a Los Angeles County Superior Court judge said not so fast.
      

            Because the judge felt there was insufficient evidence of nerve damage and other issues, they signed off on the singer's request for a new trial on damages unless Avila agreed to the lowered amount -- which, according to newly filed docs in the case, she just did.
      
    
            The new amount is broken down into the following proposed allocations -- $3.85 million for past non-economic losses, $5.4 million for future non-economic losses, and $250,000 for future medical expenses.
      
    
            Whether it's $12.9 million or $9.5 million ... that's still a pretty big payday in court.

Halle Berry's Ex
                          Accuses Her of Attacking Their 12-year-old Son
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 1, 2026

                                                                      |

                                  October 1, 2026
                                4:28 PM PDT
                                    
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
          UPDATE
  
    
            4:20 PM PT -- The court granted the temporary restraining order for Olivier ... requiring Halle to stay away 100 yards from him. She will be allowed to see their kid but only during court-ordered visitation which is two days a week and every other weekend ... until a hearing on October 16.
      
    
            3:05 PM PT -- Halle Berry and her ex-husband Olivier Martinez have been ordered to participate in confidential mediation to discuss custody, according to new legal docs obtained by TMZ.
      
    
            Halle Berry's ex Olivier Martinez has filed a temporary restraining order against her ... alleging child abuse against the 12-year-old son they share ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Olivier alleges Halle physically abused their son, Maceo, by jumping on him, putting her hands around his neck, and choking him last Saturday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He claims Maceo called him and claimed Halle had physically attacked him and put him in a chokehold. He says it's not an isolated incident and there have been previous attacks.
      

            What's more, Olivier says Halle threatened to have him deported to France and asked Maceo what their son is going to do "as a black man" to protect her from being robbed by Olivier ... who he claims she called a "white bitch."
      
    
            The filing also mentions they were home with her boyfriend Van Hunt and Maceo was playing a VR game with goggles in his bedroom when Halle allegedly entered the room in a rage ... and said he looks "so stupid" and is "such an idiot" for playing the game.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The situation allegedly escalated from there ... when Olivier claims Halle jumped on Maceo and started physically fighting with him. He says she grabbed Maceo by the neck and started choking him while shouting, "Who is dominant now?!"
      
    
            The order states she must not drink or be under the influence of alcohol or other substances in the presence of their son. And she must undergo sobriety testing before, during or after any visitation.
      
    
    
              
                
  
    
            Halle allegedly texted Olivier the next day ... saying, "I feel terrible about what happened last night as I know he does as well."
      
    
            The filing also mentions past incidents ... 5 years ago she allegedly struck him in the face. About 10 years ago, Olivier claims Halle had a violent outburst, throwing a plate with a knife and fork on top ... and in 2023, while discussing child support, she told Maceo that Olivier was "a white bitch robbing money from a black woman."
      
    
            Olivier is requesting sole custody of their son and wants the court to force Halle to stay away from him and their son. But he doesn't want their son not to have a relationship with Halle ... Olivier just wants Maceo to have space after the alleged incident.
      
    
            Story developing ...
